newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH - Telstra bill looking good.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH - Telstra bill looking good.

text.p: The Telstra privatisation bill is looking good, even though it looked thoroughly dead before Independent senator Mal Colston quit the Labor Party on budget day, August 20.
All non-government senators except Colston and the other Independent, Brian Harradine, are opposed to the Telstra sale.
But both Colston and Harradine look like voting for the bill -- and the government needs only two votes.
The likelihood of the Independents backing the bill is apparent from them having made such moderate demands.
Colston says he has several requirements, but the one he has named is employment guarantees for Telstra "operators" in regional Queensland.

As noted in Wednesday's Canberra Watch, such guarantees would be absolutely contrary to the principles of economic rationalism but, principles aside, really do not amount to much. Even if the government cannot stomach such economic irrationalism, then it might make a counter offer of some other employment guarantee that makes no imposition on Telstra.
So one can see that demand being satisfied, especially since Treasurer Peter Costello said on Wednesday the government would "certainly address" any "legitimate point" that Colston might raise.
The only reason for caution is that we do not know what other demands Colston might have.
But if the employment guarantee is any guide, the others should not be too much of a problem. And if they are, Colston might take what he can get and supply his vote anyway.
Remember, as a defector, he does not want the early election that major Senate obstruction might prompt.
Harradine says he wants Tasmania's forests looked after by the environmental fund that the government will set up if the Telstra bill gets through.
Now that doesn't look too hard at all -- we all love Tasmania's forests -- and Government Senate Leader Robert Hill virtually said so on Wednesday.
Subject only to Harradine demanding more, Hill said "I'm sure that what he is seeking will be accommodated ..."

Note the contrast between the Independents' demands and the Australian Democrats' hard bargaining, the refusal of the official opposition (Labor or coaltion) to bargain at all, and the Greens' habitual demand for the dismantling of the apparatus of the capitalist state.
Yes, it looks like a Telstra deal can be done.
